summary: Defines DHCPv4 and DHCPv6 options that give a list of IP addresses for PANA Authentication Agents. This is one of the ways a PANA client can find the authentication agents. It is a standards-track specification.

eli5.summary: When you arrive at a new network you need to know who checks passes. This lets the network hand you the addresses of the checkers.

questions: dhcp option for pana authentication agent
how does a pana client find the paa
what is the dhcp option for pana
how does a pana client find a paa
subtitle: Two DHCP options that hand a network client the addresses of its PANA authentication agents.

tldr.problem: A PANA client joining a network needs to find a PANA Authentication Agent (PAA) to authenticate to, and needs some way to learn where one is.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 5192 defines a DHCPv4 option (code 136) and a DHCPv6 option (code 40), each carrying an ordered list of PAA addresses that the client tries in order.
tldr.outcome: DHCP is only one of several ways to locate PAAs, and the options must not be used to negotiate whether PANA is used at all, because DHCP is usually unprotected.

today: RFC 5192 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It remains the definition of the DHCP options for locating PANA Authentication Agents, which pair with the protocol in RFC 5191.

sections.title: Finding the Authentication Agent
sections.content:
RFC 5191 defines PANA, a lower layer for the Extensible Authentication Protocol (EAP) that runs over IP between a PANA Client (PaC) and a PANA Authentication Agent (PAA). Before they can talk, the client has to find a PAA.

RFC 5192 specifies DHCPv4 and DHCPv6 options that let a PaC discover PAAs. This is one of the methods for locating PAAs, not the only one.

The options are used only for discovery. They MUST NOT be used to negotiate whether PANA is used between the PaC and a PAA.
sections.eli5: Before you can show your pass you must know where the guard is standing. This document is a note the network gives you with the guard's address.

sections.title: PaC and PAA
sections.content:
The PANA Client (PaC) is the client side of the protocol and lives in the access device, such as a laptop or PDA. It provides the credentials that prove its identity so network access can be authorized. The PaC and the EAP peer sit in the same device.

The PANA Authentication Agent (PAA) is the entity in the access network that verifies the credentials and authorizes network access. The PAA and the EAP authenticator, and optionally the EAP server, are colocated in the same node.
sections.eli5: The PaC is you with your pass. The PAA is the guard at the door who checks it.

sections.title: The DHCPv4 Option
sections.content:
The DHCPv4 option carries a list of 32-bit IPv4 addresses of PAAs available to the client. Its option-code is OPTION_PANA_AGENT (136). The option-length is the length of the address list in octets and MUST be a multiple of four.

The addresses are listed in order of preference. A client SHOULD ask for the option in a Parameter Request List. A server that is configured with PAA addresses SHOULD send the option even if the client did not ask for it.

A client that receives the option SHOULD use the addresses to locate PAAs, and MUST try them in the order listed.
sections.eli5: The network gives you a list of guard addresses, best one first. You ask them in that order.

sections.title: The DHCPv6 Option
sections.content:
The DHCPv6 option works the same way but carries 128-bit IPv6 addresses. Its option-code is OPTION_PANA_AGENT (40), and the option-length MUST be a multiple of sixteen.

A DHCPv6 client SHOULD request the option in an Options Request Option (ORO). A configured server SHOULD send it even if it was not requested. The client SHOULD use the addresses to locate PAAs and MUST try them in the listed order.
sections.eli5: Same note, but written with the longer kind of address used by the newer network.

sections.title: IANA Option Codes
sections.content: IANA assigned the option name OPTION_PANA_AGENT the value 136 for DHCPv4 (described in Section 4) and the value 40 for DHCPv6 (described in Section 5). The same name is used in both protocols, but the numbers differ because each protocol has its own option number space.
sections.eli5: Each kind of network keeps its own phone book of option numbers, so the same option has a different number in each.

sections.title: Rogue Agents and Bidding Down
sections.content:
The security considerations of the DHCP RFCs apply. If an attacker modifies a DHCP response or inserts its own, a PaC could be led to contact a rogue PAA, which might intercept authentication requests or deny the device network access.

In most networks the DHCP exchange before network access authentication is neither integrity protected nor origin authenticated. For that reason the options MUST NOT be used to negotiate PANA. Treating the presence or absence of the option as a signal that the network requires PANA (or not) is an example of what is forbidden, since it would allow bidding-down attacks that push clients to a weaker security mechanism, or none.
sections.eli5: A stranger could slip you a note pointing to a fake guard. So the note may say where guards are, but must never decide whether you need to show a pass.
